Q1286.t: A white crescent across the heart of Europe
Q1286.s: From cruise height the Alps look like crumpled white paper laid across Europe: sharp ridges, dark valleys and glaciers poured into the gaps. The arc runs about 1,200 km, from the Mediterranean near Nice almost to Vienna. Even Mont Blanc, the highest summit at about 4,800 m, sits some six kilometres below you.
Q1286.w: White ridges broken by deep valleys, with long lakes such as Garda, Como and Geneva at their feet.
f: The Aletsch Glacier in Switzerland is the longest in the Alps: about 20 km of ice.
Around 14 million people live in the Alps.
The Gotthard Base Tunnel, opened in 2016, runs 57 km beneath the Alps — the longest railway tunnel in the world.

q.q: Which is the longest glacier in the Alps?

Q5451.t: The highest wall on Earth, almost at your altitude
Q5451.s: No other mountains come this close to your wing. The Himalayas rise from the green plains of India in steps — foothills, forested ridges, then a white wall — and Everest, at 8,849 m, reaches to within about two kilometres of cruise height. The range is still growing as India keeps pushing north into Asia.
Q5451.w: A white wall of peaks between the green plains of India and the brown, high Tibetan Plateau.
f: Himalaya means “abode of snow” in Sanskrit.
Ten of the world’s fourteen peaks above 8,000 m are in the Himalayas; the other four are in the Karakoram.
Marine fossils are found near Everest’s summit: its top layers are limestone laid down on an ancient sea floor.

q.q: What does the Sanskrit name “Himalaya” mean?

Q5456.t: A 7,000-km spine down the whole of South America
Q5456.s: Seven thousand kilometres long, the Andes change character as you fly along them: glaciers and fjords in Patagonia, a wall of snow above Santiago, and in Bolivia a high plateau, the Altiplano, where Salar de Uyuni lies like a sheet of white paper. No mountain chain on any continent is longer.
Q5456.w: Snowy peaks and volcanic cones on one side, desert or rainforest on the other; in Bolivia, dazzling white salt flats.
f: Aconcagua, at 6,961 m, is the highest mountain outside Asia.
Salar de Uyuni is so flat that it is used to calibrate satellite altimeters.
La Paz, in the Bolivian Andes at around 3,600 m, is the highest seat of government in the world.

q.q: Which is the highest peak of the Andes?

Q5463.t: Where North America’s rivers choose their ocean
Q5463.s: Somewhere along these ridges runs the Continental Divide: rain on one side flows to the Pacific, on the other towards the Atlantic or the Arctic. From the air the Rockies are range after range of grey-brown peaks, dark with pine forest and streaked with snow well into summer. They stretch some 4,800 km, from northern British Columbia to New Mexico.
Q5463.w: Parallel ridges of grey rock and dark forest, snowfields on the peaks, and flat sagebrush basins between the ranges.
f: Mount Elbert in Colorado, 4,401 m, is the highest peak of the Rockies.
Yellowstone, in the Wyoming Rockies, holds about half of the world’s active geysers.
By mountain standards the Rockies are young: their main uplift began around 80 million years ago.

q.q: Which is the highest peak of the Rocky Mountains?

Q42070.t: Stony, cold and vast — a desert of dinosaur eggs
Q42070.s: Expect beige, grey and rust rather than golden dunes: most of the Gobi is bare rock and gravel, scored by dry riverbeds. It is a cold desert, lying high on a plateau across Mongolia and northern China, with winters that can drop below −30 °C. Sand seas do exist, in patches, and from above they stand out as golden ripples in the grey.
Q42070.w: Flat grey-brown gravel plains with dry riverbeds, patches of golden dunes and white salt pans.
f: In 1923 explorers at the Gobi’s Flaming Cliffs found nests of eggs that were the first to be recognised as dinosaur eggs.
In Badain Jaran, in the Chinese Gobi, dunes rise to about 500 m, with small lakes lying between them.
Wild Bactrian camels survive in the Gobi; they are a separate species, not runaway domestic camels.

q.q: What covers most of the Gobi’s surface?

Q6583.t: Almost the size of the USA — and once green
Q6583.s: You can fly for hours and still be over the Sahara. At about 9 million km² it is the largest hot desert on Earth, painted in every shade from white salt to black basalt and orange sand. Dunes cover only part of it; the rest is stony plateaus, gravel plains and dark volcanic mountains.
Q6583.w: Endless tan and orange ground: look for rippled dune fields, dark volcanic massifs and pale dry lakebeds.
f: Until about 5,000 years ago much of the Sahara was savanna with lakes; rock paintings show giraffes and cattle.
Saharan dust blown across the Atlantic helps fertilise the Amazon rainforest.
“Sahara” simply comes from the Arabic word for “desert”, so “Sahara Desert” says the same thing twice.

q.q: What does the name “Sahara” mean in Arabic?

Q5474.t: Celestial Mountains around a lake that never freezes
Q5474.s: Tian Shan means “Celestial Mountains” in Chinese, and from above the name fits: snowy ranges roll for some 2,500 km across Central Asia. In their Kyrgyz heart lies Issyk-Kul, a deep blue lake about 180 km long sitting at 1,600 m. Despite the altitude and harsh winters, it never freezes — its water is slightly salty.
Q5474.w: Rows of snowy ridges running east–west; north of them, the long blue oval of Issyk-Kul.
f: Jengish Chokusu, also called Victory Peak, is the highest summit of the Tian Shan at 7,439 m.
Issyk-Kul is one of the deepest lakes in the world, reaching about 670 m.
Khan Tengri glows pinkish-red at sunset because its summit pyramid is made of marble.

q.q: Which Tian Shan lake never freezes despite its altitude?

Q35600.t: A modest ridge that divides two continents
Q35600.s: Don’t expect peaks: the Urals are so old and worn down that from cruise height they look like low, forested wrinkles. Yet this line, running some 2,500 km from the Arctic to the steppes of Kazakhstan, is where Europe traditionally ends and Asia begins. Around Yekaterinburg the mountains are so low that the Trans-Siberian crosses them almost unnoticed.
Q35600.w: A band of dark taiga and low ridges running north–south; east of Yekaterinburg and Chelyabinsk, a scatter of lakes.
f: The Urals rose around 300 million years ago, when Europe and Siberia collided — long before the Alps existed.
The highest peak, Narodnaya, reaches only 1,895 m.
The malachite columns of St Isaac’s Cathedral in St Petersburg are faced with stone from the Urals.

q.q: Which is the highest peak of the Urals?

Q5477.t: A snowy wall between the Black Sea and the Caspian
Q5477.s: Between two seas rises a single, sharp-edged barrier: the Greater Caucasus runs about 1,200 km from the Black Sea to the Caspian, with a white crest along its spine. In the east, over Dagestan, it breaks into a maze of deep canyons and high plateaus. Elbrus, a dormant volcano with two summits, is usually counted as Europe’s highest peak at 5,642 m.
Q5477.w: A continuous line of snowy peaks running north-west to south-east between two seas.
f: Dagestan means “land of mountains”, and more than 30 languages are spoken in its valleys.
Elbrus’s two summits stand about 1.5 km apart and differ in height by only about 20 m.
Kazbek, 5,054 m, is also an old volcano; its white cone rises above the Darial Gorge.

q.q: Which peak is usually counted as Europe’s highest?

Q60140.t: A former island continent that crashed into Asia
Q60140.s: The land below you was once an island continent. Tens of millions of years ago it drifted north across the ocean and rammed into Asia, crumpling the crust into the Himalayas — and it is still pushing, a few centimetres a year. From above, look for the flat Ganges plain in the north and the old, worn Deccan plateau in the south.
Q60140.w: Flat, intensely farmed plains in the north; brown plateaus, rivers and reservoirs further south; at night, countless clusters of lights.
f: The Indian plate still moves north by about 5 cm a year.
The Deccan Traps, layers of lava up to 2 km thick, poured out about 66 million years ago.
Around a quarter of all people on Earth live on the subcontinent.

q.q: Which mountains rose when India collided with Asia?

Q31945.t: The world’s largest peninsula, tilted towards the Gulf
Q31945.s: Seen from above, Arabia is a giant tilted slab: mountains rise along the Red Sea in the west, and the land slopes gently east to the Gulf. In between lie gravel plains, black lava fields and the dunes of the Empty Quarter. Saudi Arabia, which fills most of the peninsula, has no permanent rivers at all.
Q31945.w: Beige plains and orange dune seas, dark mountain ridges along the Red Sea coast and black lava fields inland.
f: At more than 3 million km², Arabia is the largest peninsula on Earth.
Arabia is slowly pulling away from Africa: the Red Sea widens by about a centimetre a year.
The Empty Quarter in its south is the largest continuous sand desert on Earth.

q.q: Which is the largest peninsula in the world?

Q27611.t: A land bridge built by volcanoes
Q27611.s: Two oceans, one narrow strip of land: on a clear day you may see water on both sides of the plane. A chain of volcanoes runs along the Pacific side, many of them near-perfect cones, while the Caribbean coast is low, green and swampy. When this land bridge closed about 3 million years ago, animals began crossing between the Americas.
Q27611.w: A string of volcanic cones along the Pacific coast, with lakes such as Nicaragua and Atitlán shining between them.
f: Lake Nicaragua is the largest lake in Central America, and bull sharks swim in it.
Tajumulco in Guatemala, 4,220 m, is the highest peak in Central America.
Guatemala alone has more than 30 volcanoes.

q.q: Which Central American lake is home to bull sharks?

Q185605.t: Antarctica’s long finger pointing at South America
Q185605.s: Ice-capped mountains, glaciers spilling into the sea and a coast shattered into islands: the Antarctic Peninsula reaches some 1,300 km north towards Cape Horn. It is the mildest and most visited corner of the continent, and one of the fastest-warming places on Earth. Along its eastern side, vast ice shelves float on the Weddell Sea.
Q185605.w: Jagged, snow-covered peaks along a narrow spine, and glaciers flowing into a dark sea dotted with icebergs.
f: In 2002 part of the Larsen Ice Shelf larger than Luxembourg broke apart in about five weeks.
The Drake Passage between the peninsula and Cape Horn is about 800 km wide.
Most tourists who reach Antarctica come here, on ships from Ushuaia.

q.q: Which sea lies east of the Antarctic Peninsula?

Q319671.t: A 3,500-km wall holding back the polar ice
Q319671.s: Dark rock peaks break through the white here, marking one of the longest mountain ranges on Earth. The Transantarctic Mountains cross the whole continent, splitting East Antarctica from West, and hold back the thick East Antarctic ice sheet like a dam. Glaciers squeeze through the gaps between the summits and flow down to the Ross Ice Shelf.
Q319671.w: Rows of dark, flat-topped peaks poking through the ice, with broad glaciers flowing between them.
f: Both Shackleton and Scott reached the polar plateau by climbing the Beardmore Glacier, about 200 km long.
Bones of a crested dinosaur, Cryolophosaurus, were found high on Mount Kirkpatrick in this range.
Coal seams and fossil Glossopteris leaves found here show that Antarctica was once forested.

q.q: Which glacier did Shackleton and Scott climb to the polar plateau?

Q192583.t: Australia’s green seam between coast and outback
Q192583.s: This is less a wall than a long, worn backbone: the Great Dividing Range runs some 3,500 km down eastern Australia, and from the air you notice the change of colour more than the mountains. On the coast side lie green forest and river valleys; inland, the land fades to dry brown plains. Its western rivers flow away from the nearby sea, towards the Murray–Darling or the dry heart of the continent.
Q192583.w: Green, forested ridges near the east coast; inland of them, farmland and scrub turning to brown plains.
f: Mount Kosciuszko, 2,228 m, is its highest point and the highest in mainland Australia.
The Blue Mountains near Sydney are part of the range; their blue haze comes from eucalyptus oil in the air.

q.q: Which is the highest peak of the Great Dividing Range?

Q21195.t: A peninsula still rising after the Ice Age
Q21195.s: From cruise height Scandinavia is a mosaic of dark forest and countless lakes, with mountains along the Norwegian side and deep fjords cutting into the Atlantic coast. All of it once lay under an ice sheet up to about 3 km thick. Freed of that weight, the land is still rebounding — in places by nearly a centimetre a year.
Q21195.w: Dark green forest speckled with hundreds of lakes; to the west, snowy mountains and fjords like narrow blue cracks.
f: Sweden’s High Coast has risen about 285 m since the ice melted, the greatest such rebound known.
Sweden alone has close to 100,000 lakes.
At North Cape the midnight sun shines for more than two months each summer.

q.q: Why is the land of Scandinavia still rising?
q.a: The weight of Ice Age ice has gone

Q27617163.t: Between India and China, a land of ridges and rivers
Q27617163.s: Its old name, Indochina, says it all: the land between India and China. From above you can read its structure — long mountain ridges fanning south from the Himalayas, with great rivers in the valleys between. The Mekong, Chao Phraya, Salween and Irrawaddy all run roughly north to south. In the dry season, smoke from burning fields often softens the view.
Q27617163.w: Parallel green ridges running north–south, brown rivers winding between them, rice fields shining in the valleys.
f: Cambodia’s Tonle Sap River reverses its flow every rainy season, and the lake it drains swells several times over.
The Mekong flows through or along six countries: China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam.
Thailand and Vietnam are among the world’s largest rice exporters.

q.q: Which river reverses its flow every rainy season?

Q12837.t: A sun-baked tableland at the edge of Europe
Q12837.s: On the map Iberia is almost a square, and much of its interior is a lofty tableland, the Meseta, where ochre wheat fields and olive groves run to the horizon. Mountain ranges ring it and cross it, and the Pyrenees seal it off from the rest of Europe. At the southern tip, only about 14 km of sea separate it from Africa.
Q12837.w: Ochre and green plains broken by bare, rocky sierras, and reservoirs with branching, finger-like shapes.
f: Madrid, at about 650 m, is one of the highest capital cities in Europe.
Spain has more than 1,000 large dams, one of the highest counts in the world.
Near Almería, plastic greenhouses cover so much land that they show up as a white patch from space.

q.q: How wide is the Strait of Gibraltar at its narrowest?

Q181528.t: The Sahara’s driest corner, where years pass without rain
Q181528.s: This eastern part of the Sahara, spread across Egypt, Libya and Sudan, is among the driest places on Earth — some spots go years without a drop of rain. From above it is a study in beige: flat gravel plains, the long parallel dunes of the Great Sand Sea, and the brown sandstone plateau of the Gilf Kebir rising like an island.
Q181528.w: Pale sand drawn into long, straight dune lines running north–south, and the dark, flat-topped Gilf Kebir plateau.
f: A carved piece of yellow Libyan desert glass, found only in this region, sits in a pectoral from Tutankhamun’s tomb.
The Cave of Swimmers in the Gilf Kebir has ancient paintings of people who seem to be swimming — in today’s driest desert.

q.q: Whose tomb held a jewel set with Libyan desert glass?

Q37056.t: Where Eurasia runs out of land
Q37056.s: You are over the very top of Eurasia. Taymyr’s tip, Cape Chelyuskin, is the northernmost point of any continent’s mainland; across a narrow strait lie only the islands of Severnaya Zemlya and the pack ice. Below you: treeless tundra, the low Byrranga Mountains and a web of lakes and rivers that stay frozen for most of the year.
Q37056.w: Flat, treeless tundra laced with lakes, and the long, low ridges of the Byrranga Mountains running east–west.
f: Musk oxen, gone from here for thousands of years, were brought back from Canada and Alaska in the 1970s and thrived.
Taymyr is home to the largest herd of wild reindeer in Eurasia.
Cape Chelyuskin was first reached in 1742 by Semyon Chelyuskin, travelling by dog sled.

q.q: What is the northernmost point of mainland Eurasia?

Q488266.t: “The end of the land”, freckled with countless lakes
Q488266.s: In the Nenets language Yamal means “the end of the land”, and from above the name feels right: a flat, pale tundra reaching north into the Kara Sea, so pocked with lakes that it seems more water than ground. Nenets herders still cross it with their reindeer, travelling hundreds of kilometres each year between summer and winter pastures.
Q488266.w: A flat peninsula between the Kara Sea and the Gulf of Ob, scattered with thousands of round lakes.
f: Beneath Yamal lie some of the largest natural gas fields on Earth.
In 2014 a crater tens of metres wide appeared in the tundra, blown out by gas from thawing permafrost.
The peninsula is about 700 km long.

q.q: What does “Yamal” mean in the Nenets language?

Q993.t: A land of fire and ice on the edge of the Pacific
Q993.s: White cones, one after another, some trailing a thin plume: Kamchatka has around 30 active volcanoes, one of the densest clusters on Earth. On a clear day you can pick out several at once, rising from dark forest and tundra. The tallest, Klyuchevskaya Sopka, reaches about 4,750 m — the highest active volcano in Eurasia.
Q993.w: Snow-capped volcanic cones in a row along the peninsula’s spine and east coast, often with steam or ash at the top.
f: The Valley of Geysers, discovered in 1941, is one of the largest geyser fields in the world.
Kamchatka is about 1,200 km long, yet no road links it to the rest of Russia.
The Volcanoes of Kamchatka have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996.

q.q: Which is the highest active volcano in Eurasia?

Q18758.t: Asia’s long green tail, reaching for the equator
Q18758.s: Mainland Asia ends at the tip of this peninsula, barely 150 km from the equator. From above, its spine is a line of rainforest-covered mountains; on either side the green turns into the neat, dotted rows of oil palm and rubber plantations. Off the west coast runs the Strait of Malacca, busy with ships day and night.
Q18758.w: A forested mountain spine down the middle, geometric plantations on both sides, and ships dotting the Strait of Malacca to the west.
f: Tanjung Piai, at the peninsula’s tip, is the southernmost point of mainland Asia.
The Strait of Malacca is one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world.
Gunung Tahan, 2,187 m, is the highest peak of Peninsular Malaysia.

q.q: Which is the southernmost point of mainland Asia?

Q319288.t: Africa’s rooftop, where the Nile gets its flood
Q319288.s: A vast green-and-brown plateau, mostly above 1,500 m, rises out of the surrounding lowlands like a fortress. Its flat tops are farmed right to the edge, then drop into canyons — the Blue Nile Gorge is up to 1.5 km deep. Every summer, monsoon rain on these highlands sends down the flood that has fed Egypt for millennia.
Q319288.w: A high tableland of fields and eucalyptus groves, split by deep brown canyons; Lake Tana shines to the north.
f: Most of the Nile water that reaches Egypt falls as rain on the Ethiopian Highlands.
Arabica coffee comes from here: it still grows wild in Ethiopia’s forests.
Addis Ababa, at about 2,350 m, is one of the highest capital cities in the world.

q.q: Which lake is the source of the Blue Nile?

Q167021.t: Mountains folded like a rumpled carpet
Q167021.s: From above, the Zagros are one of the clearest pictures of how mountains are made: long parallel ridges curve for hundreds of kilometres like folds in a pushed rug, as Arabia presses into Iran. In the south, dark round blotches stand out between the folds — salt domes, where ancient salt has squeezed up through the rock and flowed out like a glacier.
Q167021.w: Long, curving parallel ridges like wrinkles in cloth, with round dark salt domes between them near the Gulf coast.
f: The Zagros run about 1,500 km, from near the Turkish border to the Strait of Hormuz.
The Middle East’s first oil strike came in the Zagros foothills, at Masjed Soleyman, in 1908.
Goats were domesticated in the Zagros around 10,000 years ago.

q.q: Which collision is folding up the Zagros?

Q5955.t: Golden mountains where four countries meet
Q5955.s: Snowy peaks, turquoise rivers and larch forest shading into steppe: the Altai sit in the middle of Asia, where Russia, Kazakhstan, China and Mongolia come together. Look for the milky turquoise ribbon of the Katun River and the long, narrow blade of Lake Teletskoye. Belukha, the highest peak at 4,506 m, wears a white, twin-headed cap all year.
Q5955.w: White peaks above dark larch forest, the turquoise Katun River and the narrow blue strip of Lake Teletskoye.
f: The Golden Mountains of Altai have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998.
Ancient Pazyryk burials, sealed in permafrost, preserved tattooed human skin about 2,400 years old.
Belukha is the highest point in Siberia.

q.q: Which is the highest peak of the Altai?

Q293713.t: The ridge where forest ends and the steppe begins
Q293713.s: Look for a sharp change of colour: the Greater Khingan divides the damp, green Manchurian side in the east from the dry grasslands of the Mongolian Plateau in the west. The range itself is gentle, rarely much above 2,000 m, but it catches the summer monsoon and casts a rain shadow over the steppe beyond. It runs about 1,200 km from north to south.
Q293713.w: Low, forested ridges running north–south, with greener fields to the east and tawny steppe to the west.
f: Its northern slopes carry one of China’s largest forests, mostly of larch.
West of the range lie the Hulunbuir grasslands, some of the finest pastures in China.

q.q: What lies to the west of the Greater Khingan?

Q214284.t: A remote divide between the Arctic and the Pacific
Q214284.s: Dark taiga, bare stony summits and barely a road: the Stanovoy Range is one of Siberia’s emptiest places. It is the region’s great watershed — rivers on its north side flow to the Lena and the Arctic, those on the south to the Amur and the Pacific. In winter the ridges turn white and the valleys vanish under snow.
Q214284.w: Long, dark-green ridges with pale rocky tops running east–west, and winding rivers in empty valleys.
f: For nearly two centuries after the 1689 Treaty of Nerchinsk, these mountains roughly marked the border between Russia and China.
The railway to Yakutsk crosses the range near Neryungri, a coal-mining town in southern Yakutia.

q.q: Which great river takes the water from the Stanovoy’s north side?

Q26813923.t: The Himalayas’ first and youngest wrinkle
Q26813923.s: Coming from the Indian plains, these are the first hills you meet: low, green, steep-sided ridges rising abruptly from the flat Terai. The Siwaliks are the youngest and outermost fold of the Himalayas, made of gravel and sand washed down from the high peaks and then pushed up again. Behind them rise higher ranges, and on a clear day the snows.
Q26813923.w: The first line of low, forested hills rising sharply from the flat, farmed plain, parallel to the snowy peaks beyond.
f: The name is usually explained as “belonging to Shiva”.
Their rocks are rich in fossils of ancient apes, elephants and giraffes, some more than 10 million years old.
In Nepal these hills are called the Chure range.

q.q: Where do the Siwalik Hills lie within the Himalayas?

Q161750.t: The Roof of the World, cut by giant glaciers
Q161750.s: Locals called it Bam-i-Dunya, the Roof of the World, and from the air it looks the part: a high, bare knot of mountains where the Tian Shan, Hindu Kush and Karakoram all meet. In the eastern Pamirs even the valley floors lie around 4,000 m. The Fedchenko Glacier, more than 70 km long, is the longest glacier outside the polar regions.
Q161750.w: A dense knot of snowy peaks and long glaciers; to the east, high, bare brown plateaus with turquoise lakes.
f: Ismoil Somoni Peak, 7,495 m, is the highest point of the Pamirs.
Lake Karakul, at about 3,900 m, fills a crater left by a meteorite impact millions of years ago.
The Pamir Highway crosses the Ak-Baital Pass at about 4,650 m, one of the highest roads in the world.

q.q: What is the traditional nickname of the Pamirs?

Q5472.t: A snowy wall on the old roads of Central Asia
Q5472.s: A sea of sharp, snowy peaks cut by deep valleys stretches about 800 km from central Afghanistan into northern Pakistan. For thousands of years traders, pilgrims and armies threaded the Hindu Kush’s high passes between Central Asia and India. Tirich Mir, the highest summit at 7,708 m, rises near its eastern end.
Q5472.w: Row upon row of jagged white peaks, with narrow green valleys and braided grey rivers deep below.
f: Lapis lazuli mined in these mountains for more than 6,000 years ended up in the jewellery of Egyptian pharaohs.
Alexander the Great crossed the Hindu Kush on his way to India in the 4th century BC.

q.q: Which is the highest peak of the Hindu Kush?

Q5469.t: K2’s kingdom of rock, ice and giant glaciers
Q5469.s: Few places outside the polar regions hold this much mountain ice: glaciers such as the Siachen and the Baltoro, each over 60 km long, fill the Karakoram’s valleys like frozen motorways striped with dark rock. Above them stand K2 and three more peaks over 8,000 m. The name is usually translated from Turkic as “black gravel”.
Q5469.w: Long, straight glaciers with dark stripes of rock down their middle, between clusters of sharp granite peaks.
f: K2, 8,611 m, is the second-highest mountain on Earth.
Some Karakoram glaciers have held steady or even grown while most mountain glaciers shrink — the “Karakoram anomaly”.
The Karakoram Highway crosses the range at the Khunjerab Pass, about 4,700 m high.

q.q: Which is the second-highest mountain on Earth?

Q187871.t: The stern northern rampart of the Tibetan Plateau
Q187871.s: Look for the line where the sand stops. The Kunlun rise like a rampart along the northern edge of the Tibetan Plateau, with the yellow Tarim Basin and the Taklamakan desert at their feet and cold, high Tibet behind them. The range runs some 3,000 km, and in Chinese myth its peaks were the home of immortals.
Q187871.w: A sharp boundary: a yellow desert basin on the north side, snow-streaked grey ridges and the high plateau to the south.
f: The Qinghai–Tibet Railway crosses the Kunlun at a pass about 4,770 m high.
Nephrite jade from the Kunlun rivers near Hotan has been prized in China for thousands of years.
In Chinese legend the Kunlun were the home of Xiwangmu, the Queen Mother of the West.

q.q: Which basin lies at the northern foot of the western Kunlun?

Q130135.t: The barrier between the Mediterranean and the Sahara
Q130135.s: Green on one side, red and ochre on the other: the Atlas Mountains hold back the Sahara from the Mediterranean coast for some 2,500 km, from Morocco’s Atlantic shore to Tunisia. Their northern slopes catch rain and even snow, while the southern flanks look scorched. In the Middle Atlas, dark cedar forests shelter the Barbary macaque, the only macaque living in Africa.
Q130135.w: Snow-dusted ridges with dark cedar forest on the north side, and bare red and ochre slopes on the Saharan side.
f: Jebel Toubkal, 4,167 m, in the High Atlas, is the highest peak in North Africa.
The Atlas cedar grows wild only in these mountains of Morocco and Algeria.
The mountains are named after Atlas, the Titan of Greek myth who holds up the sky.

q.q: Which is the highest peak of the Atlas Mountains?

Q93332.t: Ancient ridges combed into parallel lines
Q93332.s: Look down for stripes: in the Ridge-and-Valley country the Appalachians form long, forested ridges running side by side for hundreds of kilometres, as if the land had been combed. These are some of the oldest mountains on Earth, raised more than 250 million years ago and once far higher than today. Erosion has worn them down to rounded, green hills.
Q93332.w: Long, parallel forested ridges with farmed valleys between them, running south-west to north-east.
f: The Appalachian Trail follows the range for about 3,500 km, from Georgia to Maine.
The Blue Ridge owes its blue haze to natural compounds released by its trees.
Mount Mitchell in North Carolina, 2,037 m, is the highest peak in the eastern United States.

q.q: Why do the Blue Ridge Mountains look blue?
q.a: Haze from compounds released by trees

Q929910.t: America’s wild northern rampart above the Arctic plain
Q929910.s: Above the Arctic Circle, the Brooks Range sweeps across northern Alaska for about 1,000 km: grey, treeless peaks, braided rivers and hardly a settlement anywhere. To the north the land drops to the flat Arctic coastal plain, dotted with countless lakes. In summer the snow melts from the valleys; in winter everything lies white under a low sun.
Q929910.w: Grey, jagged, treeless ridges running east–west and wide braided riverbeds; to the north, flat tundra full of lakes.
f: Gates of the Arctic National Park, in the Brooks Range, has no roads or trails at all.
The Trans-Alaska Pipeline crosses the range at Atigun Pass, about 1,400 m high.
Its crest divides rivers flowing to the Arctic Ocean from those heading to the Bering Sea.

q.q: Which pipeline crosses the Brooks Range at Atigun Pass?

Q920070.t: Ice, rainforest and fjords on Canada’s Pacific edge
Q920070.s: Between the Pacific and the interior of British Columbia rises a wall of granite peaks and icefields some 1,600 km long. Fjords push deep inland between them, and their lower slopes are cloaked in dense temperate rainforest. On a clear day you look down on glaciers feeding milky rivers that wind to the sea.
Q920070.w: Jagged snowy peaks and icefields, with long fjords and green valleys cutting in from the Pacific coast.
f: Mount Waddington, 4,019 m, is the highest peak lying entirely within British Columbia.
The range is built largely of granite and forms one of the largest granite bodies on Earth.
The Skeena and Stikine rivers slice right through the range on their way to the Pacific.

q.q: Which is the highest peak lying entirely within British Columbia?

Q4558.t: A line of lone white volcanoes above dark forest
Q4558.s: The Cascades are easy to spot: a chain of big, isolated snow cones — Baker, Rainier, Adams, Hood, Shasta — standing high above the forest from British Columbia to northern California. Between them, the range is dark green on its rainy western side and brown and dry on the east. In the north, the jagged North Cascades hold hundreds of glaciers.
Q4558.w: Solitary white volcanic cones in a north–south line far above the forest; green western slopes, dry brown eastern ones.
f: Mount Rainier, 4,392 m, carries more glacier ice than any other peak in the contiguous United States.
Crater Lake in Oregon fills the collapsed top of a Cascade volcano and is the deepest lake in the US, about 590 m.
The range is named after the cascades of the Columbia River, where it cuts through the mountains.

q.q: Which lake fills the collapsed top of a Cascade volcano?

Q156684.t: Home of Denali, North America’s giant
Q156684.s: Even from cruise height Denali looks enormous: at 6,190 m it is North America’s highest peak, and it rises from lowlands only a few hundred metres above sea level, so its full bulk is on show. Around it the Alaska Range curves some 650 km across southern Alaska, a white wall of ice and rock above spruce forest and tundra.
Q156684.w: One massive white peak towering above all the others, with long glaciers streaming from a curved wall of snowy summits.
f: From base to summit Denali rises about 5,500 m — more than Everest does above the Tibetan Plateau.
The Kahiltna Glacier, the climbers’ route to Denali, is about 70 km long.
The mountain has two names in use: Denali and Mount McKinley.

q.q: How high is Denali, North America’s highest peak?

Q40556.t: Africa’s sharp eastern tip, jutting into the ocean
Q40556.s: On the map it is exactly what its name says: a horn thrust out into the sea. The Horn of Africa juts east between the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean — a dry land of red-brown plains, thorny scrub and long, straight beaches. From above it is mostly ochre, crossed by the green threads of the Shabelle and Juba rivers.
Q40556.w: Ochre and red-brown plains with sparse scrub, a long sandy coastline, and thin green ribbons along the rivers.
f: Ras Hafun in Somalia is the easternmost point of mainland Africa.
Somalia has the longest coastline of any country on the African mainland, over 3,000 km.
Frankincense and myrrh, prized in the ancient world, come from trees that grow wild on the Horn’s dry hills.

q.q: Which is the easternmost point of mainland Africa?

Q23522.t: A knot of mountains wrapped in blue seas
Q23522.s: Look down and you’ll see why travel here was always slow: the Balkan Peninsula is a jumble of mountain ranges, deep valleys and high basins, with the Adriatic on one side and the Aegean and Black Sea on the other. The main north–south routes follow the valleys of the Morava and the Vardar. The peninsula takes its name from the Balkan Mountains in Bulgaria.
Q23522.w: Tightly packed green and grey ridges, small basins with towns and fields, and deep river valleys running north–south.
f: The word “Balkan” is usually traced to a Turkish term for a chain of wooded mountains.
Musala in Bulgaria, 2,925 m, is the highest peak of the peninsula, just ahead of Mount Olympus.
Lake Ohrid is one of the oldest lakes in Europe, more than a million years old.

q.q: Which is the highest peak of the Balkan Peninsula?

Q1359850.t: Kazakhstan’s “Hungry Steppe”, flat to every horizon
Q1359850.s: Between the Chu River and Lake Balkhash lies a clay-and-gravel plateau so empty that it is also known as the Northern Hungry Steppe. From above it is a vast, flat sheet of grey-beige, crossed by faint tracks and dotted with white salt pans. Only in spring, for a few short weeks, does a green tinge spread across it.
Q1359850.w: A featureless grey-beige plain with white salt pans; Lake Balkhash to the north-east, the Chu River’s green thread to the south-west.
f: Betpak-Dala is home to one of Kazakhstan’s main herds of saiga, the antelope with a trunk-like nose.
The desert covers about 75,000 km².

q.q: Which animal with a trunk-like nose roams Betpak-Dala?

Q169132.t: The Land of Five Rivers, a patchwork of fields
Q169132.s: Punjab means “five waters” in Persian, after the five rivers — the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej — that cross this flat plain to join the Indus. From above it is one of the most intensely farmed landscapes on Earth: a fine patchwork of wheat and rice fields laced with a dense grid of irrigation canals. At night, towns and villages sparkle everywhere.
Q169132.w: A flat, finely divided patchwork of green and gold fields, straight canals and wide, braided riverbeds.
f: The Indus basin irrigation network, fed by Punjab’s rivers, is one of the largest in the world.
Lahore, on the Ravi, is famous for its Mughal fort and Shalimar Gardens, both listed by UNESCO.
Punjab is often called the breadbasket of the subcontinent.

q.q: What does the name Punjab mean?

Q229269.t: The Empty Quarter: the largest sand sea on Earth
Q229269.s: Nothing but sand for hundreds of kilometres: the Rub’ al Khali, the Empty Quarter, is the largest continuous sand desert in the world, about 650,000 km². From above, look for giant dunes lined up like waves, some over 200 m high, with pale salt flats in the hollows between them. Its colours shift from yellow to deep orange-red.
Q229269.w: Endless rows of orange dunes like frozen waves, with white or grey salt flats in the corridors between them.
f: In 1930–31 Bertram Thomas made the first recorded crossing by a Westerner, travelling by camel.
Wilfred Thesiger crossed it twice in the 1940s and described it in his classic book “Arabian Sands”.
The Rub’ al Khali is larger than France.

q.q: What does the name “Rub’ al Khali” mean?

Q375816.t: Brazil’s “white forest” that turns green in days
Q375816.s: In the dry season the Caatinga looks grey and lifeless from above: thorny scrub that has dropped every leaf, dotted with cacti. Its name comes from the Tupi for “white forest”. But when the rains arrive, the whole landscape flushes green within days. This semi-arid land of north-eastern Brazil exists nowhere else on Earth.
Q375816.w: Grey-brown scrubland in the dry season, bright green after rain, with reservoirs shining like scattered mirrors.
f: The Caatinga is the only major biome that lies entirely within Brazil.
The mandacaru, a tall columnar cactus, is a symbol of this dry back country, the sertão.
Serra da Capivara, in the Caatinga, has one of the largest concentrations of prehistoric rock art in the Americas.

q.q: What does the Tupi name “Caatinga” mean?

Q47700.t: Rust-red sand beneath a sea of grass and thorn
Q47700.s: The Kalahari is not the bare dune field you might imagine: its deep red sand is held down by grass and thorn trees, so from above it looks like rust-coloured ground brushed with pale green. Long parallel dunes run for kilometres, lined up by the wind. Far to the north, the same sand swallows the Okavango River, which never reaches the sea.
Q47700.w: Red-brown ground speckled with grey-green scrub, long straight dune ridges and white pans of dry salt lakes.
f: The Okavango Delta, where a river vanishes into the Kalahari sand, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The sand’s red colour comes from a thin coating of iron oxide on each grain.
The San people have lived in the Kalahari for many thousands of years.

q.q: Which river ends in the Kalahari without reaching the sea?

Q2913098.t: Dark peaks stranded in a white ocean of ice
Q2913098.s: Here the Transantarctic Mountains fray into their last, lonely ranges: dark summits and ridges sticking out of an endless white sheet, near the inner edge of the Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf. The Pensacola Mountains stretch some 450 km. They were discovered only in 1956, spotted from a US Navy aircraft.
Q2913098.w: Scattered dark rock ridges and peaks poking through flat, endless white ice.
f: The mountains are named after the US Naval Air Station at Pensacola, Florida.
The Dufek Massif in this group is one of the largest layered igneous intrusions on Earth.

q.q: What are the Pensacola Mountains named after?

Q1139110.t: The roof of Antarctica, crowned by Mount Vinson
Q1139110.s: The highest mountains of the coldest continent rise here as a sharp, dark crest above the West Antarctic ice. Their Sentinel Range holds Mount Vinson, Antarctica’s highest peak at 4,892 m, and a string of other summits over 4,000 m. From above, the black rock faces and long glaciers stand out sharply against the white.
Q1139110.w: A sharp north–south line of dark peaks and ridges above flat white ice, with long glaciers streaming off both sides.
f: Lincoln Ellsworth discovered the range in 1935, during the first flight across Antarctica.
Climbers reach Vinson via a seasonal camp on the Union Glacier, where planes land on bare blue ice.

q.q: Which is the highest peak in Antarctica?

Q1796029.t: Amundsen’s stairway to the South Pole
Q1796029.s: In November 1911 Roald Amundsen and his team climbed through these mountains with their dog sledges, up the steep Axel Heiberg Glacier to the polar plateau. From here the South Pole lies only about 400 km away. From above, the Queen Maud Mountains are a jumble of dark peaks and broad glaciers pouring down to the flat Ross Ice Shelf.
Q1796029.w: Dark, rugged peaks between wide glaciers that flow north onto the smooth white Ross Ice Shelf.
f: Amundsen named the range after Queen Maud of Norway.
The Axel Heiberg Glacier is named after a Norwegian brewer who helped pay for Amundsen’s expeditions.
Amundsen’s team reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911.

q.q: Which glacier did Amundsen climb through these mountains?

Q842139.t: A misty green spine that hid an unknown animal
Q842139.s: Cloud often clings to this long green spine between the Mekong valley and the coast of Vietnam. The Annamites run some 1,100 km along the border of Laos and Vietnam, their steep forested ridges so remote that in 1992 scientists discovered a large mammal entirely new to science: the saola, a shy forest ox with long, straight horns.
Q842139.w: Steep, forest-green ridges, often capped with cloud, separating the hills of Laos from Vietnam’s narrow coastal plain.
f: In Vietnamese the range is called Truong Son, “the long mountains”.
Son Doong cave, in Vietnam’s Phong Nha–Ke Bang park in these mountains, has the largest known cave passage in the world.

q.q: Which large mammal was discovered in the Annamites in 1992?

ne-rg-1730074073.t: An ocean of green threaded with brown rivers
ne-rg-1730074073.s: Below you the Amazon rainforest — the selva — rolls to every horizon, a green so continuous it looks like moss. The only breaks are rivers: wide, coffee-coloured and looping back on themselves, leaving crescent-shaped lakes where old bends were cut off. In the afternoon, towering rain clouds bubble up over the canopy.
ne-rg-1730074073.w: Unbroken green canopy, brown rivers in huge loops and crescent-shaped oxbow lakes; in the afternoon, storm towers above.
f: Iquitos, in the Peruvian selva, is often called the largest city in the world that cannot be reached by road.
Upstream of Iquitos, the Marañón and Ucayali rivers join to form the Amazon.
In Spanish, selva simply means “forest” or “jungle”.

q.q: Which two rivers join in Peru to form the Amazon?

Q748435.t: Genghis Khan’s sacred mountains, birthplace of rivers
Q748435.s: Here the Siberian taiga reaches south into Mongolia: dark larch forest on the slopes, open grassy valleys below. The Khentii are the heartland of the Mongols — Burkhan Khaldun, the mountain Genghis Khan is said to have worshipped, rises among them. Three great rivers, the Onon, Kherlen and Tuul, begin in these hills.
Q748435.w: Dark forested ridges with open, grassy valleys; Ulaanbaatar spreads along the Tuul at the south-western edge.
f: The Great Burkhan Khaldun Mountain was listed by UNESCO in 2015 as a sacred landscape.
The Kherlen flows east into Lake Hulun in China, while the Onon becomes part of the Amur system.

q.q: Which sacred Khentii mountain is linked to Genghis Khan?

Q22449163.t: Remote northern ranges famous for green jade
Q22449163.s: Rounded grey peaks, dark spruce valleys and hardly a light at night: the Cassiar Mountains straddle the border of northern British Columbia and Yukon. Their rocks hold rich deposits of nephrite jade, making this one of the world’s main sources of the green stone. Few roads cross them; the Stewart–Cassiar Highway winds past the hamlet of Jade City.
Q22449163.w: Rounded grey-green peaks, broad forested valleys and scattered lakes, with no towns in sight.
f: Jade City, a tiny settlement on the Stewart–Cassiar Highway, sells nephrite mined in these mountains.
The Cassiar gold rush of the 1870s first drew miners into these remote valleys.

q.q: Which green stone is mined in the Cassiar Mountains?

Q1774690.t: Kenya’s only true desert, a salt-white ancient lakebed
Q1774690.s: East of Lake Turkana the land flattens into a pale, almost white expanse: the Chalbi, often called Kenya’s only true desert. It is the floor of an ancient lake, and after rare rains it floods into a shallow sheet of water before drying back to a cracked, salty crust. Gabbra herders bring their camels to the few oases on its edge.
Q1774690.w: A flat, pale grey-white basin east of jade-green Lake Turkana, with the forested hump of Mount Marsabit to the south-east.
f: Lake Turkana, just to the west, is the largest permanent desert lake in the world.
The Chalbi is so flat and bare that heat mirages often make it look like a lake even when it is dry.

q.q: Which big lake lies just west of the Chalbi Desert?

Q624170.t: Dark mountains between the Nile and the Red Sea
Q624170.s: Unlike the sandy west, Egypt’s Eastern Desert is a land of jagged, dark mountains and dry valleys — wadis — running down to the Red Sea on one side and to the Nile on the other. From above, look for the sudden contrast: turquoise sea, a thin strip of coast, then a chaos of brown and black peaks. The ancient Egyptians mined gold here.
Q624170.w: Jagged brown and black mountains cut by pale, branching wadis, with the turquoise Red Sea along the eastern edge.
f: The Turin Papyrus Map, drawn about 1150 BC, shows quarries and gold mines here — perhaps the oldest geological map known.
The Romans quarried rare purple porphyry for their emperors at Mons Porphyrites, in these mountains.

q.q: Which rare stone did the Romans quarry in the Eastern Desert?

Q22041906.t: A lava plateau in southern Brazil, cut by sheer canyons
Q22041906.s: About 130 million years ago, as South America and Africa began to split, lava flooded this region layer after layer, building a plateau more than a kilometre thick in places. Its edge, the Serra Geral, drops in steep escarpments split by deep canyons such as Itaimbezinho. On top, look for dark stands of Paraná pine among the fields.
Q22041906.w: A high, flat plateau of fields and dark pine groves ending in steep cliffs and canyons; its rivers flow west, away from the sea.
f: The Iguaçu Falls pour over the same layers of basalt, on the plateau’s western side.
The Paraná pine, whose flat-topped crowns dot the plateau, belongs to a tree family that grew alongside the dinosaurs.
The same lava flows appear across the ocean in Namibia, torn apart when the Atlantic opened.

q.q: Which famous waterfall pours over the same basalt layers?

Q22529966.t: Snowy ranges and long lakes in Canada’s inland rainforest
Q22529966.s: West of the Rockies, British Columbia’s interior rises into another tangle of snowy ranges — the Selkirks, Monashees, Purcells and Cariboos, together called the Columbia Mountains. Between them lie long, narrow lakes such as Kootenay, Arrow and Slocan, like strips of blue ribbon. The western slopes catch so much snow and rain that they grow a rare inland rainforest of giant cedars.
Q22529966.w: Tight clusters of snowy peaks separated by long, narrow blue lakes running north–south, with dark forest on the slopes.
f: Rogers Pass, where the railway and the Trans-Canada Highway cross the Selkirks, gets about 10 m of snow in a typical winter.
The Columbia River loops right around the northern Selkirks in a giant curve known as the Big Bend.
Their eastern edge is the Rocky Mountain Trench, a straight valley hundreds of kilometres long.

q.q: Which pass takes the railway and highway across the Selkirks?

Q747843.t: Mongolia’s green heart, where an empire’s capital stood
Q747843.s: In the middle of Mongolia the land lifts into the Khangai: broad, rounded mountains where larch forest clings only to the north-facing slopes, so the hills look striped dark and light. Herders have grazed these pastures for thousands of years. At the range’s eastern foot, in the Orkhon Valley, stood Karakorum, the 13th-century capital of the Mongol Empire.
Q747843.w: Broad, rounded mountains with dark forest on the north slopes and pale grass on the south, and green river valleys between.
f: The Orkhon Valley, with the ruins of Karakorum, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Otgontenger, the highest peak of the Khangai, is revered by Mongolians as a sacred mountain.
Rivers from the Khangai’s northern slopes flow through the Selenga into Lake Baikal.

q.q: Which old imperial capital stood at the foot of the Khangai?

Q863798.t: The wall that splits China into north and south
Q863798.s: Cross this range and you cross a climate line: the Qinling split China into a dry, wheat-growing north and a wet, rice-growing south. From above, yellow loess and the plain of Xi’an lie on one side, green terraced valleys on the other. In the bamboo forests on its slopes live giant pandas and golden snub-nosed monkeys.
Q863798.w: A long east–west wall of forested ridges, with brownish plains around Xi’an to the north and greener hills to the south.
f: Together with the Huai River, the Qinling mark China’s traditional boundary between north and south.
Taibai Shan, about 3,770 m, is the highest peak in the eastern half of mainland China.
Xi’an, at the range’s northern foot, was the starting point of the Silk Road.

q.q: Which river pairs with the Qinling as China’s north–south line?

Q20155858.t: A stone desert as flat and dark as a slate roof
Q20155858.s: Not every desert is sand. A hamada is a bare, rocky plateau swept clean by wind, and the Hamada du Draa is a classic: a vast, flat pavement of dark stones south of the Draa valley. From above it looks like slate or scorched leather, broken only by dry riverbeds. Along its northern edge runs the Draa, a river that rarely reaches the sea.
Q20155858.w: A dark, flat stony plain to the horizon, cut by pale dry riverbeds, with the green Draa oases to the north.
f: The Draa is Morocco’s longest river, about 1,100 km, yet it reaches the Atlantic only in rare wet years.
Desert varnish — a thin dark film of manganese and iron — gives the hamada’s stones their black sheen.

q.q: What is a hamada?

Q272521.t: A desert within the desert, once home to the loneliest tree
Q272521.s: Ténéré means “desert” in the Tuareg language — a desert within the Sahara. East of the Aïr Mountains it spreads as a vast, smooth sea of pale sand, some of the flattest and emptiest land on Earth. For decades a single acacia stood here, the only tree for some 400 km and a landmark for caravans, until a truck knocked it down in 1973.
Q272521.w: An immense, smooth sheet of pale yellow sand with few landmarks; the dark Aïr Mountains rise along its western edge.
f: What remains of the Tree of Ténéré stands in the National Museum in Niamey; a metal sculpture marks its old spot.
At Gadoufaoua the shifting sands have uncovered dinosaur skeletons and the giant crocodile Sarcosuchus.
Salt caravans still cross the Ténéré to the oasis of Bilma.

q.q: What happened to the famous Tree of Ténéré in 1973?

Q307143.t: A golden sea of dunes, frozen mid-storm
Q307143.s: Few views from the air say “Sahara” like this one: a golden sea of dunes stretching across eastern Algeria into Tunisia. Look for the patterns — long ridges, crescents and, in places, huge star-shaped dunes with arms radiating from a peak. Beyond its northern edge, the white salt crust of Chott el Djerid gleams in the sun.
Q307143.w: Golden dunes in regular patterns — ridges, crescents and stars — with the white salt flat of Chott el Djerid to the north.
f: Sets for Tatooine, the desert planet of Star Wars, were built near Tozeur and Nefta on the erg’s Tunisian edge.
“Erg”, a word taken from Arabic, is what geographers call a large sea of dunes.
Hassi Messaoud, Algeria’s largest oilfield, lies at the erg’s western edge; at night its gas flares glow.

q.q: Which film saga shot desert scenes on the erg’s Tunisian edge?

Q2064799.t: The Sahara’s great empty basin, far from any oasis
Q2064799.s: Here lies one of the most remote corners of the Sahara: El Djouf, a vast basin of dunes and gravel on the border of Mauritania and Mali, with no roads, villages or permanent wells across much of it. From above, look for endless parallel dune ridges running north-east to south-west, combed by the steady trade wind. Its Arabic name means “the belly” — a hollow in the desert.
Q2064799.w: Endless parallel orange dune ridges and gravel plains, with no roads, towns or green patches anywhere in sight.
f: On its north-eastern edge lies Taoudenni, where salt has been cut in slabs and carried by camel to Timbuktu for centuries.
The French naturalist Théodore Monod spent decades exploring this empty basin by camel.

q.q: Which salt-mining oasis lies on El Djouf’s north-eastern edge?

Q855658.t: A high desert of cactus, gypsum dunes and the Rio Grande
Q855658.s: Much of the Chihuahuan Desert lies on high plateaus between two Mexican mountain ranges, so it is cooler than you might expect, and most of its rain falls in summer storms. From above it is a mosaic of tan basins, dark volcanic hills and dry lakebeds. On the Texas border the Rio Grande makes its Big Bend, carving deep canyons through the ranges.
Q855658.w: Tan basins with dark volcanic hills and pale dry lakebeds; the Rio Grande’s green ribbon winds through canyons.
f: White Sands, at the desert’s northern end in New Mexico, is the largest gypsum dune field in the world.
The Chihuahuan Desert is one of the richest places on Earth for cactus species.

q.q: Which field of white gypsum dunes lies in the Chihuahuan Desert?

Q189429.t: The land of the saguaro, surprisingly green
Q189429.s: For a desert, the Sonoran looks surprisingly green from above: two rainy seasons a year feed a dense scatter of shrubs, trees and giant cacti. It spreads across Arizona, California and north-western Mexico, broken by rugged little mountain ranges. Look for the sharp green squares of irrigated farms along the Colorado and Gila rivers, and the vast grid of Phoenix to the east.
Q189429.w: Olive-dotted desert basins between small, jagged ranges, bright irrigated fields along the rivers, and Phoenix’s sprawling grid.
f: The giant saguaro cactus grows wild almost only in the Sonoran Desert.
A saguaro can grow more than 12 m tall and live for over 150 years.
Phoenix, in the heart of the desert, is one of the largest cities in the United States.

q.q: Which giant cactus is the symbol of the Sonoran Desert?

Q1670841.t: A desert cradled in the Yellow River’s great loop
Q1670841.s: Look for the Yellow River swinging north in a huge, almost rectangular loop: the land inside it is the Ordos Plateau, and its sandy south is the Mu Us Desert. Over recent decades much of the Mu Us has been fixed with planted shrubs and trees, so from above you may see as much grey-green as yellow. The Great Wall once ran along its southern edge.
Q1670841.w: A plateau of pale sand patches and grey-green scrub inside the Yellow River’s big loop, crossed by straight roads.
f: Kubuqi, the desert on the northern side of the Ordos, is known for huge solar farms laid out on the sand.
The Ordos Plateau is rich in coal, making it one of China’s main energy regions.

q.q: Which river loops around the Ordos Plateau?

Q132956.t: A sea of shifting sand ringed by snowy mountains
Q132956.s: The Taklamakan fills the Tarim Basin like sand poured into a bowl: dunes in every direction, walled in by the snowy Tian Shan to the north and the Kunlun to the south. It is one of the largest shifting-sand deserts on Earth. Old Silk Road oases such as Kashgar and Hotan ring its edges, fed by meltwater streams that die out in the sand.
Q132956.w: Huge dune fields in a closed basin, ringed by snowy mountains and green oasis strips where rivers leave the foothills.
f: The name is popularly translated as “go in and you won’t come out”, though its real origin is uncertain.
The Tarim Desert Highway crosses the dunes for more than 500 km, protected by planted belts of shrubs.
The Tarim River, fed by mountain meltwater, runs along the desert’s northern edge and never reaches the sea.

q.q: Which mountains wall in the Taklamakan to the north?

Q483134.t: A mountainous peninsula with a rugged eastern spine
Q483134.s: About 70% of the Korean Peninsula is hills and mountains, and from above you can see how they crowd towards the east: a long spine, the Baekdudaegan, runs close to the eastern coast, while the land slopes west to broad plains and a shore of islands and vast mudflats. In autumn the forests turn every shade of red and gold.
Q483134.w: Forested ridges crowding the east coast, flatter farmland and cities in the west, and a western shore of islands and mudflats.
f: The tidal flats of the west coast are a UNESCO World Heritage Site; tides there can rise more than 8 m.
From north to south the peninsula is about 1,000 km long.

q.q: Roughly how much of the Korean Peninsula is mountainous?

Q584279.t: North Africa’s highest wall, snow above the desert
Q584279.s: From Marrakesh you can see its snow in winter, and from above the High Atlas is a sharp, rust-and-white barrier running some 700 km across Morocco. To the north lie green plains and the Atlantic; to the south the desert begins almost at once. Deep gorges such as Todgha and Dadès cut its southern flank, with thin green strips of palm oases below.
Q584279.w: A rust-red mountain wall topped with snow in winter; narrow green oasis strips wind along the valleys on its southern side.
f: The road from Marrakesh to Ouarzazate crosses the range at the Tizi n’Tichka pass, about 2,260 m high.
Aït Benhaddou, a fortified earthen village on the southern side, is a UNESCO site and a favourite film location.

q.q: Which pass carries the road from Marrakesh to Ouarzazate?

Q183295.t: The Dragon Mountains, a basalt wall around Lesotho
Q183295.s: Seen from above, the Drakensberg is a single colossal cliff: the edge of a high basalt plateau that drops more than a kilometre to the green hills of KwaZulu-Natal. On top lies Lesotho, a mountain kingdom where even the lowest ground is about 1,400 m above sea level. In winter the rim of the escarpment is often dusted with snow.
Q183295.w: A long, dark escarpment edge: a flat, bare high plateau on one side, folded green foothills far below on the other.
f: Its Zulu name, uKhahlamba, means “barrier of spears”; Drakensberg is Afrikaans for “dragon mountains”.
Thabana Ntlenyana in Lesotho, 3,482 m, is the highest peak in southern Africa.
The Maloti-Drakensberg Park holds thousands of rock paintings made by the San people.

q.q: What does the Zulu name uKhahlamba mean?

Q5191296.t: Green hills where Central Africa’s rivers rush to the sea
Q5191296.s: A band of low, rainforest-covered hills runs parallel to the Atlantic coast of Central Africa, from Equatorial Guinea through Gabon towards the mouth of the Congo. Rivers crossing it tumble down in rapids, and the mighty Congo itself breaks through in the Livingstone Falls, a chain of cataracts below Kinshasa. From above it is an almost unbroken carpet of dark green.
Q5191296.w: Low, rolling hills under dense green rainforest a short way inland from the Atlantic, with brown rivers cutting through them.
f: Gabon’s Monts de Cristal National Park, at the northern end of the range, is one of Africa’s richest places for plant species.
Below Kinshasa the Congo drops about 270 m through the Livingstone Falls on its way to the ocean.

q.q: Which cataracts carry the Congo through these hills to the sea?

Q309104.t: Dark volcanoes rising from the heart of the Sahara
Q309104.s: In the middle of the Sahara, dark volcanic mountains rise out of the sand like islands. The Tibesti in northern Chad holds the highest summit of the Sahara, Emi Koussi, at about 3,400 m — a huge shield volcano whose crater is some 12 km across. Nearby lies Trou au Natron, a deep caldera whose floor is streaked white with salt.
Q309104.w: Dark brown and black volcanic massifs rising from pale sand, with wide craters and white salt crusts inside some calderas.
f: Trou au Natron is about 1 km deep, and its floor is crusted with white natron salt.
Rock art in the Tibesti shows cattle and giraffes from the time when the Sahara was green.

q.q: Which is the highest summit of the Sahara?

Q23836082.t: Black volcanic spires in the heart of the Algerian Sahara
Q23836082.s: Out of the Algerian Sahara rises the Ahaggar, or Hoggar: a high granite plateau crowned with dark volcanic peaks and needle-like plugs of old lava, weathered into fantastic shapes. It is the home ground of the Tuareg, and the town of Tamanrasset sits at its foot. Its highest peak, Mount Tahat, reaches about 2,900 m.
Q23836082.w: A dark, rugged highland of black peaks and spires rising from pale desert, with dry valleys radiating outwards.
f: On the Assekrem plateau, about 2,700 m up, stands the hermitage the French monk Charles de Foucauld built in 1911.
Wild Saharan olive trees survive in the Ahaggar’s high valleys, relics of a wetter past.

q.q: Which is the highest peak of the Ahaggar?

Q170383.t: Dark granite islands in a sea of sand
Q170383.s: The Aïr rises from the Sahara like a cluster of dark islands: granite massifs, some almost perfectly round, surrounded by yellow sand. The rings are the roots of ancient volcanoes laid bare by erosion, and they show up clearly from the air. Between them, dry valleys hold acacias and a few Tuareg villages; the old caravan town of Agadez lies at the southern edge.
Q170383.w: Dark, rounded rock massifs, some ring-shaped, standing out against pale sand, with the smooth Ténéré dunes to the east.
f: The Aïr and Ténéré Natural Reserves together form one of the largest protected areas in Africa, listed by UNESCO.
The old town of Agadez, with its tall mud-brick minaret, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q.q: Which caravan town lies at the southern edge of the Aïr?

Q404600.t: Forested hills that the Amur River slices in two
Q404600.s: Low, rolling and dark with forest, the Lesser Khingan rise between the plains of Manchuria and the Amur. The range is modest, mostly under 1,000 m, but here the great Amur cuts straight through it in a narrow, winding gorge. The hills are covered with Korean pine, larch and birch, turning gold and red in autumn.
Q404600.w: Low, dark-green forested hills with the broad Amur River squeezing through them in a winding gorge.
f: At the range’s western foot lies Wudalianchi, a cluster of volcanoes that last erupted in 1719–21, damming a chain of five lakes.
Korean pine, whose seeds are sold as pine nuts, is one of the range’s main trees.

q.q: Which great river cuts through the Lesser Khingan in a gorge?

Q155322.t: Tiger country on Russia’s Pacific shore
Q155322.s: A long, forested range runs some 1,000 km along Russia’s Pacific coast, north of Vladivostok. Its forests are unique: northern taiga mixes with southern broadleaf woods, Amur tigers share them with brown and Himalayan bears, and spruce grows beside wild grapes and lianas. From above it is a sea of ridges, dark green in summer and flecked with gold in autumn.
Q155322.w: Endless parallel forested ridges between the Ussuri valley and the sea, with small river mouths along the coast.
f: On 12 February 1947 one of the largest iron meteorite showers ever seen fell here, leaving dozens of craters.
Central Sikhote-Alin is a UNESCO World Heritage Site that protects the Amur tiger’s home.

q.q: What fell on the Sikhote-Alin in February 1947?

Q215917.t: A frozen arc beside the Pole of Cold
Q215917.s: A great arc of bare, jagged mountains curves some 1,200 km along the east bank of the lower Lena, rising steeply above its broad, braided valley. Beyond the range lie Verkhoyansk and Oymyakon, the coldest inhabited places in the Northern Hemisphere, where winter can bring −67 °C. In summer the snow retreats to the summits; in winter everything is white and silent.
Q215917.w: A long wall of grey, snow-streaked peaks east of the wide, braided Lena, with empty, larch-dotted valleys between them.
f: Verkhoyansk, beyond the range, recorded −67.8 °C in 1892, one of the lowest temperatures ever measured in an inhabited place.
Summer there can top +30 °C — a swing of about 100 degrees across the year.
Permafrost beneath the range reaches hundreds of metres deep.

q.q: Which town beyond the range is famed as a Pole of Cold?

Q1072879.t: A snowy wall above the Silk Road’s Hexi Corridor
Q1072879.s: Along the north-eastern edge of the Tibetan Plateau, the Qilian Mountains form a long snowy wall, their glaciers feeding the rivers that water the Hexi Corridor below. That narrow strip of oases, squeezed between the mountains and the Gobi, was the main route of the Silk Road into China. At the range’s northern foot, the Zhangye hills are striped red, orange and yellow.
Q1072879.w: A long, white-capped range to the south, a green strip of oases and fields along its foot, and the grey-brown Gobi beyond.
f: The Hexi Corridor was the main Silk Road route between China’s heartland and Central Asia.
Jiayuguan fort, the western end of the Ming Great Wall, stands at the foot of the Qilian.

q.q: Which Silk Road corridor runs along the Qilian’s northern foot?

Q1156557.t: Green hills between the Yangtze and the Huai
Q1156557.s: Between the Yangtze and the Huai River, the Dabie Mountains rise as a forested knot of peaks in central China, often wrapped in mist. They look gentle from above — green ridges, terraced tea slopes and reservoirs in the valleys — but their rocks tell a violent story: they were dragged more than 100 km down into the Earth and then brought back up.
Q1156557.w: A compact cluster of green, forested ridges with reservoirs in the valleys, between two broad river plains.
f: Tiny diamonds and coesite in the Dabie rocks prove they were once buried more than 100 km deep.
The mountains divide the basins of the Yangtze and the Huai.
Lu’an Guapian, a well-known Chinese green tea, is grown on the Dabie slopes.

q.q: How deep were the Dabie Mountains’ rocks once buried?

Q1195285.t: The ridges that shield southern China from winter
Q1195285.s: Across southern China runs a jumble of rounded, forested ranges, the Nanling. They divide the Yangtze basin from the Pearl River basin and shelter Guangdong from the coldest winter winds, so subtropical crops grow on their southern side. From above, look for green hills scarred with red earth, rice terraces and, towards Guilin, jagged limestone pinnacles.
Q1195285.w: Rounded green ridges running east–west, red earth and rice terraces, and sharp limestone pinnacles to the west near Guilin.
f: Nanling simply means “southern ridges” in Chinese.
The Lingqu Canal, dug in the 3rd century BC, crossed these mountains to link the Yangtze and Pearl River systems.

q.q: Which two river basins do the Nanling divide?

Q4527.t: India’s rain-soaked green wall above the Arabian Sea
Q4527.s: Running some 1,600 km parallel to India’s west coast, the Western Ghats are the first thing the summer monsoon hits: their seaward slopes are drenched and deep green, while the land behind them lies in a rain shadow. Around the Nilgiri Hills they rise to a high, rolling plateau of tea gardens and grassland. Just to the south, the Palghat Gap cuts a rare low pass through the wall.
Q4527.w: A steep, dark-green escarpment parallel to the coast, tea gardens on the Nilgiri plateau and the wide Palghat Gap to the south.
f: The Western Ghats are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the world’s biodiversity hotspots.
The neelakurinji shrub blooms here only once every 12 years, turning whole slopes blue-purple.
Anamudi, 2,695 m, is the highest peak in India south of the Himalayas.

q.q: How often does the neelakurinji of the Western Ghats bloom?

Q465055.t: Broken hills where India’s great rivers break through
Q465055.s: Unlike the continuous wall of the Western Ghats, the Eastern Ghats are a broken chain of old, worn hills along India’s east coast. The great rivers of the Deccan — the Godavari, Krishna and Mahanadi — cut right through them on their way to the Bay of Bengal, fanning out into fertile deltas. In the north, forested hills around the Araku Valley grow coffee.
Q465055.w: Low, forested, broken hills parallel to the east coast, with wide rivers cutting through them to green deltas.
f: The Borra Caves in the Eastern Ghats are among the largest caves in India.
Chilika Lake, near the northern end of the Ghats, is India’s largest coastal lagoon.

q.q: Where do the rivers that cut through the Eastern Ghats flow?

Q271435.t: The old line between northern and southern India
Q271435.s: For centuries Indians saw the Vindhya as the dividing line between north and south — the Gangetic plains on one side, the Deccan on the other. From above it is less a range than a long, broken escarpment of flat-topped sandstone hills. Along its southern foot flows the Narmada, one of the few big Indian rivers that runs west.
Q271435.w: A long line of flat-topped, scrub-covered sandstone hills and cliffs, with the Narmada valley along the southern side.
f: The Bhimbetka rock shelters in the Vindhya foothills hold prehistoric paintings and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Buddhist stupas of Sanchi, begun in the 3rd century BC, stand on a hilltop in this region.

q.q: Which west-flowing river runs along the Vindhya’s southern foot?

Q207692.t: Red cliffs, a winding river and the home of rock tea
Q207692.s: On the border of Fujian and Jiangxi, the Wuyi Mountains rise as forested ridges and bare red sandstone cliffs. The Nine-Bend River loops between them, and on narrow terraces among the rocks grows Wuyi rock tea, including the famous Da Hong Pao. From above, look for red rock walls standing out against the deep green.
Q207692.w: Dense green forest broken by bare red cliffs and domes, with a winding river threading between them.
f: The Wuyi Mountains are a UNESCO World Heritage Site for both their nature and their culture.
Da Hong Pao tea from the few ancient bushes here has fetched record prices at auction.
The Neo-Confucian philosopher Zhu Xi taught in these mountains in the 12th century.

q.q: Which famous tea comes from the Wuyi Mountains?

Q128500.t: The marmot mountains on the Kazakh–Chinese border
Q128500.s: A long, bare ridge runs east–west along the border of Kazakhstan and China, rising abruptly from dry steppe. The Tarbagatai take their name from the Mongolian word for marmot, and those burrowing animals still whistle on the grassy slopes. To the north lies the blue sheet of Lake Zaysan; to the south, the Dzungarian Basin opens out.
Q128500.w: A lone east–west ridge, snow-streaked in winter, rising from brown steppe, with Lake Zaysan to the north-east.
f: The range’s highest point, Mount Tastau, falls just short of 3,000 m.
South of the range lies the Dzungarian Gate, a windswept pass that has long linked Central Asia and China.

q.q: Which animal gave the Tarbagatai their name?

Q682334.t: The golden mountains at the edge of Tibet
Q682334.s: Altyn-Tagh means “golden mountains” in Turkic — a fitting name for these bare, sun-baked ridges. The range forms the north-eastern rim of the Tibetan Plateau, dropping steeply to the Tarim Basin and the salt flats of Lop Nur. Along it runs a huge fault, where the plateau slides sideways past the rest of Asia.
Q682334.w: Bare, tawny ridges rising steeply south of the desert, with the pale, ear-shaped salt flats of Lop Nur to the north-east.
f: The Altyn Tagh Fault runs for about 1,600 km, one of the longest active faults in Asia.
Lop Nur, a dried-up lake, is ringed with salt bands that make it look like a giant ear from space.
The Lop Nur area is one of the last refuges of the wild Bactrian camel.

q.q: What does the name Altyn-Tagh mean?

Q186547.t: Norway’s high spine of ice, fjords and bare plateaus
Q186547.s: The Scandinavian Mountains run about 1,700 km along the peninsula, mostly through Norway. From above they are less a line of peaks than a vast, bare highland scraped by ice, scattered with lakes and snowfields and slashed on the west by deep fjords. In Jotunheimen, the “home of the giants”, the land rises to the highest summits in northern Europe.
Q186547.w: Bare grey-brown plateaus with snowfields and countless lakes, deep fjords cutting in from the west, glaciers on the highest ground.
f: Galdhøpiggen, 2,469 m, in Jotunheimen, is the highest peak in Scandinavia.
Jostedalsbreen is the largest glacier in mainland Europe.
Musk oxen roam the Dovrefjell plateau, brought back from Greenland in the mid-20th century.

q.q: Which is the highest peak in Norway?

Q1288.t: A great forested arc wrapped around Transylvania
Q1288.s: The Carpathians curve through Central and Eastern Europe in an arc about 1,500 km long, and from above you can see how they cradle the Transylvanian Basin like a horseshoe. Their slopes carry some of Europe’s largest surviving beech and spruce forests, home to many brown bears, wolves and lynx. Only in the Tatras do they rise to sharp, alpine-looking peaks.
Q1288.w: A curving band of dark-forested ridges, with the patchwork fields and towns of the Transylvanian Basin inside the arc.
f: Gerlachovský štít in Slovakia’s High Tatras, 2,655 m, is the highest peak of the Carpathians.
Romania’s Carpathians hold one of the largest brown bear populations in Europe.
The Danube cuts through the range at the Iron Gates, a gorge on the border of Serbia and Romania.

q.q: Where does the Danube cut through the Carpathians?

Q377264.t: The long, bony spine of Italy
Q377264.s: The Apennines run some 1,200 km through Italy, from Liguria to the toe of Calabria, and from above they are its unmistakable backbone: grey limestone ridges, beech forest and towns clustered on hilltops. They reach their highest in Abruzzo, at the Gran Sasso. Nearby, look for a strangely flat oval of fields ringed by mountains — the bed of Lake Fucino, drained in the 19th century.
Q377264.w: A grey-green mountain spine down the middle of Italy; in Abruzzo, the flat oval of the drained Fucino basin among the peaks.
f: Corno Grande in the Gran Sasso massif, 2,912 m, is the highest peak of the Apennines.
Under Emperor Claudius the Romans dug a 5.6-km tunnel to drain Lake Fucino, but it was fully drained only in the 1870s.

q.q: Which is the highest peak of the Apennines?

Q12431.t: A wall between Spain and France, with a country inside
Q12431.s: From the Atlantic to the Mediterranean, the Pyrenees form an almost unbroken wall about 430 km long between Spain and France. The French side is greener and steeper; the Spanish side is drier, with long ridges and ochre valleys. Tucked high in the middle is Andorra, a small country of deep valleys and ski slopes.
Q12431.w: A continuous snowy crest from sea to sea, with greener valleys on the French side and drier ochre ones on the Spanish side.
f: Aneto, 3,404 m, on the Spanish side, is the highest peak of the Pyrenees.
The waterfall in the Cirque de Gavarnie drops about 420 m, one of the tallest in Europe.
Andorra la Vella, at about 1,020 m, is the highest capital city in Europe.

q.q: Which is the highest peak of the Pyrenees?
